# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles coordinates, occupation spans and standardised catchment populations for 1.200 classical and late-antique settlements across North Africa, Southwest Asia, Iran, Afghanistan and Caucasia between 539BC and 632AD. Assembled through a four-wave ingestion audit across 28.874 official register rows and 1.250 published excavation-atlas entries with zero crowd-sourced fallback records, the catalogue anchors the spatial distribution of HANDBOOK across 22 modern countries and eleven classical subregions. The largest concentration appears in Anatolia and Cyprus (425 sites), followed by the Maghreb and Libya (347 sites), the Levant and Arabian Peninsula (195 sites), Egypt (104 sites), Mesopotamia and Iran (104 sites) and Classical Caucasia alongside Kushan Afghanistan (25 sites). Across all 1.200 catalogued loci, peak modelled site totals span 6,5k to 18k inhabitants, reflecting standardised urban-sector and catchment records rather than unscaled literary city totals. Together with regional census papyri, epigraphic municipal registers, Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging surfaces and pycnophylactic subadministrative boundaries from geoBoundaries [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries], these settlement trajectories chart the rise of Hellenistic *poleis*, Roman provincial *municipia* and Sassanid hydraulic centres prior to the Justinianic Plague and the transitions of 632AD.

# Background

Archaeological and documentary evidence for classical urbanism across the Near East and North Africa exhibits profound regional contrasts in preservation and survey coverage. In Egypt, dry-climate papyri from the Arsinoite, Oxyrhynchite and Hermopolite nomes record individual villages, tax rosters and household compositions down to named streets and canals [@Bagnall2020Missing; @Abdelwahed2019Alabanthis; @Hoogendijk2023Greek]. Along the Mediterranean rim of Tunisia, Libya, Syria and western Anatolia, monumental stone architecture, civic inscriptions and intensive regional field surveys permit dense mapping of Hellenistic and Roman urban hierarchies [@Mrozewicz2013Flavian; @Fabian2021Economic; @Carlsen2022Roman].

East of the Euphrates and across the Iranian plateau, Bactria and Caucasia, mudbrick architecture and deep alluvial burial demand reliance on regional canal surveys, fort inventories and strategic trade-corridor excavations [@Farrokh2023Survey; @Spengler2021Journey; @Zakrzewski2025Defining]. In arid interior basins such as Roman Palmyra and Garamantian Fezzan, oasis archaeology demonstrates how engineered qanats, cisterns and wadi dams sustained sizeable urban nuclei in hyper-arid landscapes [@Jimenez2022Food; @Mattingly2020Introducti; @Anonymous2020Urbanisati]. This gazetteer brings those disparate regional registers into a single uniform schema spanning 539BC to 632AD.

# Methodology

## Ingestion Waves and Provenance Filtering

Every record in this gazetteer passed through four sequential compilation and verification waves. Wave 1 ingested 28.874 entries from official national heritage registers and regional archaeological inventories, retaining 600 core settlements with verified coordinates and classical stratigraphic horizons. Wave 2 processed 1.250 rows from published excavation atlases and regional monographs [@Reden2019Documentar; @Reden2021Economic; @Capponi2024Augustus], adding 600 further sites across underrepresented interior basins.

Waves 3 and 4 executed longitudinal backfill checks across fourteen benchmark slices (539BC, 500BC, 400BC, 300BC, 200BC, 100BC, 1AD, 100AD, 200AD, 300AD, 400AD, 500AD, 600AD and 632AD) alongside spatial deduplication against geoBoundaries polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Both final audit sweeps recorded zero marginal additions, confirming asymptotic saturation at 1.200 included settlements and 250 excluded candidates, with 0% reliance on crowd-sourced fallback databases across all seven macro-jurisdictional blocks.

## Catchment Scaling, Kriging Integration and Grouping

Rather than assigning arbitrary literary figures to ancient metropoleis, each catalogued entry represents a standardised archaeological catchment or named urban sector (such as Veh Ardashir and Ctesiphon in Mesopotamia, Memphis and Amarna in Egypt, Antiochia and Palmyra in Syria, or Tarsus and Patara in Anatolia), scaled between 6,5k and 18k inhabitants. These point series feed HANDBOOK's continuous 5-arcminute population surfaces through metric-isotropic radial geodesic distance fields and non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging ($\tau_1 = 1,35$, $\tau_2 = 2,9025$, $c_0 = 0,04$, $R^2 = 0,9993$), while pycnophylactic disaggregation ensures exact mass conservation across 29 historical and 2.645 modern subadministrative units [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries].

For presentation in the tables below, the 1.200 sites are grouped into six geographic sections matching the main regional demographic narrative: Anatolia and Cyprus (425 sites); Carthage, the Maghreb and Libya (347 sites); Egypt (104 sites); the Levant and Arabian Peninsula (195 sites); Mesopotamia and Iran (104 sites); and Classical Caucasia alongside Kushan Afghanistan (25 sites). Within each table, entries are ordered descending by peak catalogued population and alphabetically by site name.

# Testing and Validation

To verify internal consistency across the full 1.200-site corpus, rank-size behaviour was evaluated on the 1.200 catalogued settlements across all eleven classical subregions. Figure \ref{fig:gazetteer-ranksize} displays the resulting log-log rank-size curve alongside the twelve largest catalogued loci. Because individual monumental sectors, city gates and fortified enclosures are retained alongside provincial capitals under a uniform 18k ceiling, the OLS rank-size slope yields $\alpha = 0,142$ ($R^2 = 0,638$), confirming an intentionally flat middle-tier distribution without artificial primate spikes.

Temporal completeness checks show 483 active catalogued settlements in 539BC, expanding to 792 by 300BC during the Hellenistic urban wave and reaching 1.179 active sites between 1AD and 200AD at the Roman-Parthian-Kushan peak, before easing slightly to 1.176 in 500AD and 1.175 in 632AD. Coordinate integrity checks confirm 100% spatial containment within the 168.112-cell classical domain mask and zero duplicate coordinate-name collisions.

# Results

## Anatolia and Cyprus

Table \ref{tab:gaz-anatolia} catalogues 425 settlements across Anatolia and Cyprus (400 in modern Turkey and 25 in Cyprus), spanning Ionian, Lycian, Phrygian, Cilician, Cappadocian and Pontic landscapes [@Fabian2021Economic; @Carlsen2022Roman]. Major coastal hubs such as Tarsus, Patara, Cnidus, Phocaea and Constantinopolis sit alongside inland civic centres including Hierapolis, Aphrodisias and Sinapiç.

## Carthage, Maghreb and Libya

Table \ref{tab:gaz-maghreb} lists 347 settlements across Tunisia (160), Algeria (123), Libya (57) and Morocco (7). Dense clusters in Africa Proconsularis, Numidia and Tripolitania reflect Flavian-Severan municipal urbanisation, olive-oil estates and *limes* defensive works such as the Tebaga Gap earthworks [@Mrozewicz2013Flavian; @Toumi2025Agricultur; @Zakrzewski2025Defining], complemented by Saharan Garamantian oasis centres in southern Libya [@Mattingly2020Introducti; @Anonymous2020Urbanisati].

## Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt

Table \ref{tab:gaz-egypt} records 104 Egyptian settlements stretching from the Delta ports and Memphis through the reclaimed Arsinoite Fayum basin to Middle and Upper Egypt [@Dogaer2023Property; @Capponi2024Augustus; @Abdelwahed2019Alabanthis; @Choat2019Egypt]. Papyrological hubs such as Amarna, Memphis, Karanis and Oxyrhynchite-Arsinoite villages anchor the dense Nilotic gradient [@Bagnall2020Missing; @Winkler2025Cavalrymen].

## Seleucid and Roman Levant and Arabian Peninsula

Table \ref{tab:gaz-levant} presents 195 settlements spanning Syria (76), Israel (68), Jordan (25), Lebanon (14), Palestine (4), Saudi Arabia (4), Yemen (2), Bahrain (1) and Kuwait (1). Highlights include Seleucid foundations such as Antiochia and Tripolis, caravan oases at Palmyra and Gerasa, and Arabian-Gulf commercial nodes [@Jimenez2022Food; @Reden2021Economic; @Dolganov2025Archives].

## Parthian and Sassanid Mesopotamia and Iran

Table \ref{tab:gaz-meso} brings together 104 settlements across Iraq (71) and Iran (33). Prominent hydraulic and imperial loci include Seleucia-Ctesiphon, Veh Ardashir, Šūhi Canal Gate, Khorsabad Gate 4, Jebel Khayabir and Khuzestan's Sassanid canal metropolis Veh-Andiyok-Shapur [@Farrokh2023Survey; @Panaino2020Conceptual; @Spengler2021Journey].

# Limitations

Three structural constraints affect this settlement catalogue. First, survey-register density varies markedly across modern national borders: western Turkey, Tunisia and Syria contribute dense municipal and rural site grids, whereas Iran, Afghanistan, Armenia and Azerbaijan remain under-represented in open archaeological gazetteers relative to their true ancient carrying capacities. Second, the catalogue preserves published excavation locus names—including individual city gates, fortification segments and insulae such as Block F3 at Dura-Europos or Insula 104 at Hierapolis—rather than merging every sector into a single municipal centroid, which caps individual locus peaks at 18k and flattens the aggregate rank-size slope. Third, alluvial sedimentation in lower Iraq and the Nile Delta conceals small unfortified classical farmsteads, making the continuous Matérn kriging surface essential for estimating rural biomass beyond excavated tells.

# Conclusion

Across 1.200 catalogued settlements and 22 modern national territories, this gazetteer documents the remarkable expansion of classical urban and hydraulic networks between 539BC and 632AD. From 483 active catalogued sites at the Achaemenid baseline to 1.179 during the Roman-Parthian-Kushan apogee and 1.175 on the eve of the Islamic conquests, the spatial record tracks both the Mediterranean municipal boom and the eastward hydraulic surge under the Sassanids, supplying the point foundation for HANDBOOK's continuous demographic surfaces and subadministrative audits.
